It is named after the English astronomer Edmond Halley, who noticed in 1705 that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 were probably the same object and predicted that it would come back in 1758. It did, confirming Newton's ideas about gravity, though Halley did not live to see it. Records of its appearances go back to at least 240 BCE, in Chinese chronicles, and it is shown on the Bayeux Tapestry, from 1066.

In 1986 a fleet of spacecraft, including the European Giotto probe, studied it up close. It last passed the Sun that year, and will return in July 2061. Mark Twain was born in 1835 during one visit and died in 1910 during the next.

articles.title: Asteroid Impacts
articles.description: When space rocks hit planets.
articles.content:
Impact events are collisions between asteroids or comets and planets or moons. They have shaped every solid body in the Solar System: the craters on the Moon are the scars of them, and the Moon itself probably formed from a giant impact on the young Earth.

On Earth, about 190 impact craters have been confirmed, though erosion and oceans have erased many. The famous Meteor Crater in Arizona is about 1.2 kilometres wide, made about 50,000 years ago. The Chicxulub crater, in Mexico, about 150 kilometres wide, was created 66 million years ago by an asteroid about 10 kilometres across, which caused the mass extinction that killed the non-bird dinosaurs.

Small impacts are common, such as the Chelyabinsk meteor in 2013, but big ones are rare. Astronomers survey the sky for near-Earth objects, and in 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft successfully struck the asteroid Dimorphos and altered its orbit, the first test of defending Earth.

articles.title: The Tunguska Event
articles.description: The mysterious 1908 explosion over Siberia.
articles.content:
On the morning of 30 June 1908 a huge explosion occurred in the sky over the remote Tunguska region of Siberia, in Russia. It released energy equal to about 5 to 15 megatons of TNT, hundreds of times the power of the Hiroshima bomb, and flattened about 80 million trees over an area of about 2,150 square kilometres.

People hundreds of kilometres away saw a fireball and felt the shock wave, and the night skies over Europe glowed for days. Because the region was remote, the first scientific expedition, led by Leonid Kulik, reached the site only in 1927. To their surprise they found no crater, only fallen trees radiating outward from the centre, with a few standing upright at the centre.

Most scientists conclude that a stony asteroid, about 50 to 60 metres across, exploded in the air at a height of about five to ten kilometres, before hitting the ground. Asteroid Day, on 30 June, commemorates the event and raises awareness of asteroid impacts.

articles.title: Astronomy
articles.description: The oldest science, the study of the sky.
articles.content:
Astronomy is the scientific study of celestial objects, such as stars, planets, comets and galaxies, and of the universe as a whole. It is one of the oldest sciences: people have tracked the movements of the Sun, Moon and stars since prehistory, to make calendars, to know when to plant and harvest, and to navigate.

The Babylonians recorded eclipses, the Greeks built geometric models of the heavens, and Ptolemy's Almagest, from about 150 CE, dominated for over a thousand years. Islamic astronomers, such as those at the Maragha and Samarkand observatories, refined the observations. In 1609 Galileo turned the newly invented telescope to the sky and changed astronomy for ever.

Modern astronomy is split into branches such as astrophysics, planetary science and cosmology, and uses telescopes on the ground and in space, observing across radio waves to gamma rays. Astronomy is different from astrology, which claims that the positions of stars affect people's lives, and has no scientific support.

articles.title: Nicolaus Copernicus
articles.description: The astronomer who put the Sun at the centre.
articles.content:
Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543) was a Polish astronomer and canon of the cathedral of Frombork. He studied in Kraków, Bologna and Padua and worked as a church administrator and physician, but his passion was the sky.

For nearly 1,400 years people had accepted the model of the Greek astronomer Ptolemy, in which the Earth is at the centre of the universe. Copernicus proposed instead that the Sun is at the centre and that the Earth and other planets orbit it, and that the Earth also rotates once a day. This explained in a simple way why planets sometimes seem to move backward in the sky, an effect called retrograde motion.

His book De revolutionibus orbium coelestium was published in 1543, and legend says he was given a copy on his deathbed. The idea was slow to be accepted, but it triggered the Copernican Revolution, and led to the work of Kepler, Galileo and Newton.

articles.title: Johannes Kepler
articles.description: The astronomer who discovered the laws of planetary motion.
articles.content:
Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) was a German astronomer and mathematician. He worked as an assistant to the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe, who had the most precise naked-eye observations of his time, and inherited his data on Brahe's death in 1601.

Studying the orbit of Mars, Kepler found in 1609 that planets move in ellipses, not circles, with the Sun at one focus, and that a planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun. In 1619 he showed that the square of the time a planet takes to orbit is proportional to the cube of its distance from the Sun. These three laws of planetary motion later helped Newton develop his theory of gravity.

Kepler also wrote about optics, observed the supernova of 1604 and wrote Somnium, an early work of science fiction about a trip to the Moon. NASA's Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, discovered thousands of exoplanets and was named in his honour.

articles.title: Carl Sagan
articles.description: The astronomer who brought the cosmos to millions.
articles.content:
Carl Sagan (1934–1996) was an American astronomer, author and science communicator. He was a professor at Cornell University and worked with NASA on planetary missions, including Mariner, Viking and Voyager. His research showed that the high temperature of Venus is caused by a runaway greenhouse effect.

His television series Cosmos, broadcast in 1980, was watched by hundreds of millions of people in dozens of countries. He wrote many books, including The Dragons of Eden, which won the Pulitzer Prize in 1978, and the novel Contact, which was made into a film. He helped design the Golden Record and the plaques carried by the Voyager and Pioneer spacecraft.

In 1990 he asked NASA to turn Voyager 1's camera around to take a picture of the Earth from about six billion kilometres away, and the image, called the Pale Blue Dot, inspired his reflections on the fragility of our world. He also championed the search for extraterrestrial intelligence and warned about nuclear war.

articles.title: Ulugh Beg
articles.description: The ruler-astronomer of Samarkand.
articles.content:
Ulugh Beg (1394–1449) was a Timurid ruler and one of the most important astronomers of the 15th century. The grandson of the conqueror Timur, he governed Samarkand, in present-day Uzbekistan, and turned it into a centre of science. He built a madrasa there and gathered leading mathematicians and astronomers.

In the 1420s he constructed a great observatory, whose main instrument was a giant sextant with a radius of about 40 metres, buried in a trench in the ground, one of the largest ever built. With it he and his team measured the positions of stars with unprecedented accuracy. In 1437 they completed the Zij-i Sultani, a star catalogue of 1,018 stars, the first major catalogue since Ptolemy.

They also measured the length of the sidereal year to within about a minute of the modern value. Ulugh Beg was killed in 1449 in a power struggle instigated by his own son, and the observatory was destroyed. Its remains were rediscovered in 1908.

articles.title: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi
articles.description: The astronomer of the Maragha Observatory.
articles.content:
Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (1201–1274) was a Persian polymath, born in Tus, in present-day Iran. He worked as a scholar and adviser, and when the Mongol leader Hulagu Khan conquered Persia, al-Tusi became his trusted counsellor.

With Hulagu's support, he founded the Maragha Observatory, begun in 1259, in the town of Maragha in the region of Azerbaijan, which was the most advanced astronomical institution of its time. It had large instruments, a library said to hold about 400,000 volumes, and attracted scholars from as far as China. The team compiled the Zij-i Ilkhani, astronomical tables that were used for centuries.

Al-Tusi devised a geometric device now called the Tusi couple, which generates straight-line motion from two circular motions and was later used by Copernicus in his model of the planets. He also developed trigonometry as a separate branch of mathematics and wrote on ethics, logic and philosophy.

articles.title: The Shamakhi Astrophysical Observatory
articles.description: Azerbaijan's main observatory, named after Nasreddin Tusi.
articles.content:
The Shamakhi Astrophysical Observatory is the main astronomical observatory of Azerbaijan. It stands in the Pirgulu area, near the town of Shamakhi, at an altitude of about 1,400 metres in the mountains of the Greater Caucasus, where the air is clear and dark. It is named after Nasreddin Tusi, the medieval scholar of the Maragha Observatory.

The observatory was founded in the late 1950s and opened in 1960. Its most important instrument is a two-metre telescope made by Carl Zeiss Jena, installed in 1966, which is one of the largest in the Caucasus region. Scientists there study stars, the Sun, nebulae and galaxies, and take part in international projects.

The observatory is part of the Azerbaijan National Academy of Sciences. Shamakhi itself was the capital of the Shirvanshahs for centuries, and the mountain setting makes the area one of the best places in the country for stargazing.

articles.title: Azerbaijan in Space
articles.description: Azerbaijan's satellites and space industry.
articles.content:
Azerbaijan entered the space age in 2013, when its first telecommunications satellite, Azerspace-1, was launched on 7 February from Kourou, in French Guiana, on an Ariane 5 rocket. The satellite is placed in geostationary orbit at 46 degrees east and provides television, internet and data services to Europe, Central Asia and Africa.

The satellite operator Azercosmos was established in 2010 to manage the country's space activities. In 2014 it launched Azersky, an Earth observation satellite that takes high-resolution images used for mapping, agriculture, environmental monitoring and disaster management. A second communications satellite, Azerspace-2, was launched in 2018.

Azerbaijan is one of the few countries in the South Caucasus with its own satellites. The country also has a strong scientific tradition in astronomy, from the medieval Maragha observatory to the modern Shamakhi Astrophysical Observatory.

articles.title: Observatories
articles.description: The places where we look at the sky.
articles.content:
An observatory is a place equipped for observing the sky. The earliest were monuments that tracked the Sun: the Nabta Playa stones in Egypt, Stonehenge in England and the Caracol tower at Chichén Itzá in Mexico. In the Islamic world the great observatories of Maragha, founded in 1259, and Samarkand, in the 1420s, measured the stars with huge instruments.

In 1576 Tycho Brahe built his observatory Uraniborg on an island near Copenhagen, and in 1675 the Royal Observatory at Greenwich was founded to help sailors find their longitude. In the 19th and 20th centuries astronomers built large telescopes on mountains, away from the glare of cities and above much of the atmosphere.

Today the best sites include Mauna Kea in Hawaii, at about 4,200 metres, and the Atacama Desert in Chile, where the European Southern Observatory operates the Very Large Telescope and is building the Extremely Large Telescope, with a 39-metre mirror. Space observatories such as Hubble and Webb avoid the atmosphere altogether.

articles.title: The Fermi Paradox
articles.description: If aliens exist, where is everybody?
articles.content:
The Fermi paradox is the contradiction between the high estimated likelihood of extraterrestrial civilisations and the total lack of evidence for them. It is named after the physicist Enrico Fermi, who in 1950, in a lunchtime conversation at Los Alamos, is said to have asked where everybody is.

The reasoning goes like this: there are hundreds of billions of stars in our galaxy, many with planets, and the galaxy is over ten billion years old. That would be enough time for a civilisation to colonise it, even at a slow pace, yet we see no signs. The Drake equation, formulated by Frank Drake in 1961, is a way to estimate the number of civilisations by multiplying factors such as the rate of star formation and the fraction of planets where life arises.

Proposed answers include that life is extremely rare, that intelligence rarely evolves, that civilisations destroy themselves, that interstellar distances are too great, that they are hiding, or that we simply have not looked hard enough. Another idea is the Great Filter, a difficult step that few species pass.

articles.title: The Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence
articles.description: Listening for signals from other civilisations.
articles.content:
SETI, the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence, is the scientific effort to find evidence of intelligent life beyond Earth, by listening for radio signals or looking for laser flashes. It began in 1960, when Frank Drake pointed a radio telescope in West Virginia at two nearby stars in Project Ozma.

Scientists often search near 1,420 megahertz, the frequency of hydrogen, the most common element in the universe, which any technological species might know about. In 1974 astronomers sent the Arecibo message, a short radio signal describing humans, toward a distant star cluster. In 1977 the Big Ear telescope in Ohio detected a strong 72-second signal, which astronomer Jerry Ehman circled on the printout and marked Wow!, and it has never been repeated or explained.

From 1999 to 2020 the SETI@home project used volunteers' home computers to analyse data. In 2015 the Breakthrough Listen initiative began a 10-year, 100-million-dollar search. So far no confirmed signal has been found.

articles.title: Space Tourism
articles.description: When ordinary people fly to space.
articles.content:
Space tourism is space travel for recreation. The first paying visitor was the American businessman Dennis Tito, who in 2001 spent about a week on the International Space Station on a Russian Soyuz, for a reported 20 million dollars. Several others followed over the next years.

In 2021 a new wave of suborbital flights began. On 11 July 2021 Richard Branson flew on Virgin Galactic's SpaceShipTwo, and on 20 July Jeff Bezos flew on Blue Origin's New Shepard, which takes passengers just above the boundary of space for a few minutes of weightlessness. In September 2021 SpaceX's Inspiration4 mission carried the first all-civilian crew into orbit for three days.

Costs are still high, from hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of dollars. Companies such as Axiom Space organise private missions to the International Space Station. Critics point to the pollution and risks, and supporters say that it could bring down the costs of space travel.

articles.title: Gravity Assists
articles.description: Using a planet's gravity as a slingshot.
articles.content:
A gravity assist, or slingshot, is a manoeuvre in which a spacecraft uses the gravity of a planet or moon to change its speed and direction, without using extra fuel. As the spacecraft flies past, it borrows a tiny amount of the planet's orbital energy, and the planet's motion changes by an immeasurably small amount.

The technique is essential for exploring the outer Solar System because rockets cannot carry enough fuel. It was worked out in the 1960s, in part by the young mathematician Michael Minovitch, and first used by Mariner 10, which in 1974 flew past Venus on its way to Mercury. The Voyager probes used the alignment of the outer planets in the late 1970s to fly from Jupiter to Saturn to Uranus and Neptune.

The Cassini spacecraft flew past Venus twice, then Earth and Jupiter, to gain enough speed to reach Saturn, and the European mission BepiColombo used gravity assists to reach Mercury.

articles.title: Weightlessness
articles.description: Why astronauts float in space.
articles.content:
Astronauts on the International Space Station float, but not because there is no gravity there: at that height, Earth's gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the surface. They float because the station and everything in it is in continuous free fall, falling around the Earth and moving sideways so fast that it never hits the ground. This condition is called microgravity.

It has strange effects. Liquids form floating spheres, flames burn in a round, blue shape, and there is no up or down. Without gravity, body fluids shift toward the head, giving astronauts puffy faces and a stuffy nose, and about half of them feel space sickness at first. The spine lengthens, making them a few centimetres taller.

Long-term, muscles weaken and bones lose about 1% of their density each month, so astronauts exercise about two hours a day. Scientists study these effects to keep travellers healthy on long missions, and to learn about diseases such as osteoporosis. You can feel brief weightlessness during parabolic aircraft flights, nicknamed the vomit comet.
